Word Embeddings & Text Classification

Dense vector representations of text — vector-space models, softmax & cross-entropy, word2vec.
Where we were

Last lecture: generating language

  • Statistical language models — assign probability to text and generate new language given a prompt or prefix.
  • Tokenization — decompose raw text into its basic units, tokens, so it can be processed.
  • We gave words meaning through the context they appear in.
Where we are going

This lecture: vectors that capture meaning

  • How do we represent a word as a vector, so a machine-learning model can ingest it? (ML models eat vectors.)
  • A new class of task: not generating text, but classifying it — we grow our repertoire.
The plan Vector-space models & cosine similarity → text classification with neural networks (differentiable machines: softmax & cross-entropy) → word embeddings that marry context with the vector → text classification with embeddings.
Part I

Representing text as vectors

One-hot and bag-of-words, and comparing two texts with cosine similarity.
The simplest vector space

One dimension per token

The simplest vector space gives every token its own dimension (one-hot). A document is then just word counts — order is lost (the reversed headline gives the same vector), and the vector is huge and sparse: |V| = 22 here, but 200,019 dimensions with the GPT-4o tokenizer, almost all zero.
Comparing two pieces of text

Cosine similarity

How similar are two texts? Turn each piece of text into a vector, then compare them by the angle between them.
cos(a,b) = a · b
‖a‖ ‖b‖ ∈ [−1, 1]
“telescope finds water on a distant planet”vs“astronomers spot water on a faraway world”cos ≈ 0.82
vs“parliament votes on the new climate bill”cos ≈ 0.11
Why cosine, not the raw dot product? the dot product grows with vector length, so a longer document would look “more similar” just for being long. Cosine divides that out and compares direction only.
Part II

Softmax and cross-entropy

The classification machinery: scores → probabilities → a loss → a gradient. We reuse it for word2vec.
Question
Given a piece of text, how do we classify it into one of a fixed set of classes — science, politics, sports, movies?
A neural network reads the text and must output a decision. It turns out to be a two-step recipe: softmax then cross-entropy.
Think — then → for the pieces.
Step 1 · the network's output

A classifier outputs raw scores

The classifier reads the sentence vector x; a neural net fθ produces one number per class. These raw outputs are the logits.
A logit is just a raw score — any real number, even negative, not yet a probability. Softmax (next) turns them into probabilities. The same network reappears on every slide in this part.
Scores → probabilities

Softmax

pi = esi
∑j esj   (exponentiate, then normalise)
Same network — now the output layer is passed through softmax: exponentiate (every value positive), then divide by the total (11.58). A distribution that sums to one.
Sharpen or flatten

Temperature

pi = esi/T
∑j esj/T
Same logits, divided by T before softmax. Low T (0.3) sharpens (science → 0.96); high T (3) flattens (science → 0.38) — the LLM sampling knob.
Measuring the error

Cross-entropy

ℒ = −∑i yi log pi = −log ptrue = −log 0.64 ≈ 0.45
The truth is one-hot (green ring = true class), so only the probability on the right answer counts. Why the log? a confident right answer costs almost nothing; a confident mistake costs without bound.
From loss to gradients

The gradient is p − y

pjyjpj−yj
Science0.641−0.36raise
Politics0.230+0.23lower
Sports0.100+0.10lower
Movies0.030+0.03lower
∂ℒ/∂sj = pj − yj ,   θ ← θ − η ∇ℒ
Backprop carries p − y to every weight; after one step science rises 0.64→0.75 and the loss falls 0.45→0.29.
Using the trained model

Inference · the prediction

Frozen forward pass Weights frozen; one forward pass, no labels, no loss, no gradients — the highest probability wins.
“parliament votes on the new climate bill” → fθ → logits → softmax → politics 0.91: the argmax is the decision.
Part III

Word embeddings: word2vec

The problem with sparse vectors, what we need instead, and how word2vec learns dense, meaning-bearing vectors — reusing the softmax & cross-entropy of Part II.
Why we need better vectors

The problem with sparse one-hot vectors

  • Every pair is orthogonal — hotel and motel share no dimension, so they look as unrelated as hotel and cat.
  • Huge & sparse — vectors as wide as the vocabulary (up to millions of dims), almost all zeros.
  • No shared evidence — a classifier must learn every word on its own; seeing “planet” in training teaches it nothing about “moon”.
(whotel)ᵀ wmotel = (whotel)ᵀ wcat = 0
Why this hurts prediction: if related words had similar vectors, a classifier could generalise — evidence for “planet” would transfer to “moon”. One-hot blocks exactly that, so it needs far more data and still predicts poorly on words it saw rarely.
From local to distributed

What we need: dense vectors that encode meaning

Local (1-hot): one active dimension per word — no shared structure. Distributed: meaning is spread across ~300 features, so similar words get similar vectors — and a classifier can share evidence across them, so prediction accuracy improves. How do we learn such vectors from text alone? →
The distributional idea

Meaning from the company a word keeps

Firth, 1957 “You shall know a word by the company it keeps.” A word's company = every word within ±2 positions of it, counted across a corpus of science & politics headlines.
adistantcoldnewclimatetax
planet211000
moon211000
bill000211
Use each row of counts as the word's vector: cos(planet, moon) = 1.00 (identical company), cos(planet, bill) = 0.00. Nobody told the model planets and moons are related — meaning emerged from text alone. But the table still grows with the vocabulary and is mostly zeros → we want short, dense vectors.
Word2Vec · key idea

A word is known by the company it keeps

The duck test “If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it must be a duck.” The blanks share a context: like a __ and quacks · like a __ it must · be a __.
  • Form ⟨word, context⟩ pairs by sliding a window over the text.
  • Learn vectors so a word predicts the words around it.
  • Q: how do we turn “predict the context” into something trainable?
Manufacturing training data from raw text

Skip-gram and CBOW: two ways to use the window

window · center in boldSkip-gram   center → contextCBOW   context → center
telescope spots watertelescope→spots, telescope→water{spots, water} → telescope
telescope spots water onspots→telescope, →water, →on{telescope, water, on} → spots
telescope spots water on awater→telescope, →spots, →on, →a{telescope, spots, on, a} → water
spots water on aon→spots, →water, →a{spots, water, a} → on
water on aa→water, →on{water, on} → a
Click to slide the window position by position — the pairs accumulate. This one clause yields 14 skip-gram pairs (center → each neighbour) or 5 CBOW examples (neighbours → center). Over a corpus, raw text becomes millions of pairs — no labels needed. Skip-gram is our focus.
The whole model, as classification

Word2vec is one big multi-class classifier

The one-hot center word selects a row of E — its embedding v (the bottleneck). We score v against every column of U (one output vector per word) and softmax over the whole vocabulary: one class per vocabulary word, and the true neighbour spots should win. The same softmax & cross-entropy as Part II — scaled to |V| classes.
Input vs. output embeddings

Word2vec learns two matrices

E holds a vector for each word as a center word; U a second vector for each word as a context word — both vocab × d (here d = 2). To score one pair: look up vwater (a row of E, e.g. (0.5, 0.2)); its score for context c is the dot product uc · vwater. The input embeddings E are usually kept as the final word vectors.
How the parameters are learned

Training with gradient descent

The skip-gram softmax Score a context word c by uc · vw, then softmax over the whole vocabulary — exactly the softmax of Part II, one class per word.
P(c | w) = e uc · vw
∑k∈V e uk · vw
Loss is cross-entropy ℒ = −log P(c | w) for the real neighbour; the gradient w.r.t. the scores is again p − y. The denominator — a score over every word — is the expensive part.
Making softmax affordable

Negative sampling

Why the denominator hurts

The softmax denominator sums over all V words — with V in the millions, every update is far too expensive.

Negative sampling: score the true context word against just a few k random “negative” words (real vs. fake). Draw negatives ∝ frequency3/4; k=5–20 (small data), 2–5 (large).

ℒneg = −log σ(uo · vc) − ∑i=1k log σ(−ui · vc)
A cheap yes/no question with σ — real or fake? — replaces “which of millions is the neighbour”. Only k+1 dot products, not V. (Google News word2vec: a 3M-word vocabulary.)
Forward: a dot product then σ for each pair. Untrained, all three σ ≈ 0.5 (coin flips); the three cross-entropy terms sum to loss 2.05.
Backward: the score gradient is σ − target = p − y; by the chain rule it updates only 4 rows — vwater (a row of E) and uspots, uvotes, utax (3 rows of U). One step with η = 0.5 pulls the real pair together and the fakes apart: loss 2.05 → 1.94.
Watching it train

The space organizes itself

Start from small random 2-D vectors (before) — loss 3.09 = ln 22, exactly uniform guessing. Over 600 epochs it falls to 2.24 (after): science drifts from politics, same-company words land together — planet/moon, water/ice, parliament/senate reach cosine +1, planet/bill point apart at −0.85. Nobody set these by hand — they fell out of a prediction task, and E is just the first layer of the network.
What the vectors capture

The geometry of embeddings

Analogies become arithmetic Directions in the space encode relationships, so analogies can be solved by adding and subtracting vectors.
vec(king) − vec(man) + vec(woman) ≈ vec(queen)
  • The man → woman direction is roughly the same as king → queen.
  • Good embeddings are often pre-computed and freely available (e.g. via gensim).
Part IV

Using embeddings, and their limit

Average a sentence's vectors to classify it — and why one static vector per word is not enough.
Documents → classes

Text classification

Embed each document, then run the ordinary pipeline — train data → learning algorithm → model → predict the label (Physics · Chemistry · Maths) of a new document.
From words to documents

Representing a whole document

Bag of word-vectors Each word is a vector. Represent a document as the average (or sum) of the vectors of the words it contains.
  • Simple, fast, and surprisingly strong as a baseline document representation.
  • Order is ignored — it is still a bag — but each dimension is now semantic, not a raw word count.
  • Libraries such as gensim provide word2vec and these aggregations out of the box.
  • Train the classifier with cross-entropy and gradient p − y; that gradient can even flow back into E, fine-tuning the embeddings for the task.
One word, one vector?

The static limit

Polysemy breaks static embeddings

spots means sees in “telescope spots water” but dots in “a leopard's spots” — a static embedding gives both the same vector.

The fix: make a word's vector depend on its sentence — exactly what attention and contextual embeddings do (next lectures).

Wrap-up

Summary

Take away

Words/texts become vectors (vector-space model), compared by cosine similarity.

Softmax + cross-entropy turn a vector into a decision and a loss; the gradient is p − y.

word2vec reuses that machinery as one big multi-class classifier, made cheap by negative sampling, to learn dense embeddings; analogies become arithmetic.

Average a sentence's embeddings to classify it. The static limit motivates contextual embeddings (attention).
